In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of a stable protein complex involving XPA, XPC and the transcription/repair factor TFIIH that is formed on DNA damage in the course of nucleotide excisions repair.
the interactions between DNA lesions and the proteins involved in the NER pathway.
the interactions between DNA lesions and the human proteins involved in NER.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of a stable complex of XPA and the DNA damage is dependent on the presence of TFIIH.
the XPC protein plays a key role in the recruitment of the NER machinery to DNA lesions, while the XPA protein is required to stabilize the binding of TFIIH to damaged DNA.

XPA and TFIA are involved in the formation of a long-lived DNA-protein complex, which is a prerequisite for the subsequent steps of the NER reaction, and that the formation of this complex requires ATP and XPA, XPC and TFIIH proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TFIIH, XPA, and XPC proteins are recruited in a sequential manner to damaged DNA, and this process is dependent on the presence of the excision repair complex in the cell extract.
XPA and XPF-ERCC1 are recruited first to DNA damage, followed by the recruitment of XPC and TFIIH.

XPA is a key player in the early steps in the human NER pathway, and that XPC is necessary for the stable association of XPA with DNA damage, which in turn leads to a dose-dependent recruitment of TFIIH to the damaged DNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the XPA/TFIIH complex is a stable intermediate in the early steps (damage recognition and incision) of the NER reaction.
the formation of the long-lived XPA-TFIIH complex on damaged DNA is an early step in the repair of DNA damage.
XPA is involved in the early recognition of the damaged site in the DNA and that XPA and TFIIIH interact in a stable complex on damaged DNA.
